Dutch

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /bɪl/
  • Audio:(file)
  • Hyphenation: bil
  • Rhymes: -ɪl

Etymology 1

From Middle Dutch bille, from a Proto-Germanic *balliją n, derived from *balluz (“ball”). Cognate with Old High German arsbelli, Middle High German arsbelle, Middle Low German bille (also with -e- in ārsbelle), modern Low German Bill(e), West Frisian bil. The last two mean mostly “fleshy part of the thigh” (compare the same sense also in Low German Bolle(n), regional German Bollen). The raising e > i is considered Ingvaeonic by Philippa.

Noun

bil f (plural billen, diminutive billetje n)

  1. (usually in the plural in the Netherlands and Belgium) buttock (each of the two large fleshy halves of the posterior part of the body between the base of the back, the perineum and the top of the legs)
  2. (Suriname, metonymic) buttocks, backside, posterior

Etymology 2

Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bíþla- (“axe”), instrumental noun from *bītaną (“to bite”).[1][2]

However, compare *bilją (“blade, axe”), which could have influenced its development.

Noun

bil f (plural billen, diminutive billetje n)

  1. a hammer-like double-edged tool used by stonecutters and millers

Icelandic

Etymology

From Old Norse bil, from Proto-Germanic *bilą, of uncertain origin, though probably with original sense "giving way, failure" and related to dialectal Dutch beelen (“to repent a deal”). Related to *bilōn- (“to give way”); compare also *biliþi (“likeness, evenness”) and *bibāną (“to shiver, tremble”), the latter which Kroonen suspects is connected.[1] A relation to Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”) is particularly attractive semantically, though phonetically difficult to resolve.[2]

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): [ˈpɪːl]
  • Rhymes: -ɪːl
  • Homophone: byl

Noun

bil n (genitive singular bils, nominative plural bil)

  1. space, interval
  2. period of time, moment, space
  3. (computing) space
  4. damage, wound, nick
  5. (archaic) hesitation, break (in some action, process, etc.)

    Norwegian Bokmål

    Norwegian Wikipedia has an article on:
    Bil
    Wikipedia no

    Pronunciation

    • IPA(key): /¹biːl/, [ˈbìːl]
    • Rhymes: -iːl
    • Hyphenation: bil

    Etymology 1

    Borrowed from Danish bil, a clipping of automobil, from French automobile (“self-propelled; automobile”). The shortened form was proposed in the Danish newspaper Politiken on 14 March 1902 and is attested in Norwegian in Stavanger Aftenblad on 12 April of the same year.

    The French word was originally an adjective meaning “self-propelled”, combining auto-, from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós, “self”), with mobile, from Latin mōbilis (“movable”). The Latin adjective is formed from moveō (“to move”) with -bilis; the verb continues Proto-Italic *moweō, ultimately from a causative formation of Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move”). The further origin of Greek αὐτός (autós) is disputed.

    Compare Norwegian Nynorsk bil, Swedish bil, Faroese bilur, Icelandic bíll, Greenlandic biili and English automobile.

    Noun

    bil m (definite singular bilen, indefinite plural biler, definite plural bilene)

    1. car; automobile; a motor vehicle used to carry passengers or goods, usually with four or more wheels
      Synonym: (dated) automobil
      kjøre bil ― to drive a car
      • 1902 April 12, “Reisebreve”, in Stavanger Aftenblad‎, page 1, column 3:
        […] et saadant luskende bæst af en bil – dette er jo den nyeste benævnelse paa maskinen – tøffer forbi og oser af benzin.
        […] such a sneaking beast of a car—this is, after all, the latest name for the machine—chugs past, giving off petrol fumes.
      • 1903 June 5, “Paris—Madrid-løbet”, in Stavanger Aftenblad‎, page 2:
        […] naar en række biler passerer tæt efter hinanden ad en støvet landevei […]
        […] when a line of cars passes along a dusty country road, close behind one another […]
      • 1911 August 18, “Bilens seiersgang i vore bygder”, in Trondhjems Adresseavis‎, page 4, column 1:
        Det er et nyt bevis paa bilens seiersgang gjennem vore bygder.
        It is further proof of the car’s triumphant advance through our rural communities.
      • 1920, Vilhelm Dybwad, “Vandspandet”, in Bokken Lasson, editor, 67 viser fra det gamle Chat Noir‎, Kristiania: Jacob Dybwad, page 136:
        En bil kom ut fra sin garage, […]
        A car came out of its garage, […]
      • 1964 March 20, VG‎, page 2, column 2:
        […] enten må han la være å drikke, eller også må han la bilen stå.
        […] either he must refrain from drinking, or he must leave the car parked.
      • 1997, Knut Hamsun, edited by Harald S. Næss, Knut Hamsuns brev‎, volumes 4: 1915–1924, Oslo: Gyldendal, page 379:
        […] nu vet jeg ikke om dere kommer med Bil eller med Baat.
        […] now I do not know whether you are coming by car or by boat.
      • 2011, Simen Ekern, Roma‎, Oslo: Cappelen Damm, page 107:
        […] med den kidnappede politikeren i en gammel bil, etterfulgt av en annen gammel bil?
        […] with the kidnapped politician in an old car, followed by another old car?
      • 2012 December 4, Dagens Næringsliv:
        Norges mest solgte bil er i år Volkswagen Golf
        Norway's bestselling car this year is the Volkswagen Golf
      • 2014 December 1, NRK:
        jeg [frykter] at folk vil ta bilen isteden for å reise kollektivt
        I [fear] that people will take the car instead of using public transport
      • 2015 October 14, Fædrelandsvennen‎, page 6:
        […] vil ikke det få flere til å ta bil?
        […] won't that lead more people to travel by car?
      1. (colloquial) taxi; cab
        Synonyms: taxi, drosje
        • 1914, Sigrid Undset, Vaaren‎, Kristiania: Aschehoug, page 393:
          Og trikken stod – en hel række vogner bommende fast opover Stortingsgaten. De fik en bil.
          And the trams were at a standstill—a whole line of tramcars stuck fast up Stortingsgaten. They got a taxi.
        • 1957, Gerd Grieg, Nordahl Grieg – slik jeg kjente ham‎, Oslo: Gyldendal, page 57:
          – Kan vi ikke ta bil? sa jeg. […] Vi tar lokalbanen som går nesten til døren og koster en brøkdel.
          “Can't we take a taxi?” I said. […] “We'll take the local train, which goes almost to the door and costs a fraction as much.”
        • 2008, Kari Bøge, Komponisten‎, Oslo: Aschehoug, page 217:
          […] løfter sin mobil opp, ringer etter bil.
          […] lifts her mobile phone, calls for a taxi.
        • 2009 August 1, VG‎, page 18:
          Den siktede og drapsofferet praiet en bil ved togstasjonen i 21.30-tiden.
          The suspect and the murder victim hailed a taxi by the railway station at around 9:30 p.m.
    2. a toy car
      Synonym: lekebil
      • 1992 October 31, Bergens Tidende‎, page 64:
        At jenter leker med dukker og glansbilder og at gutter snekrer hvis de ikke leker med biler, er fast-tømrede grunnholdninger i det norske samfunn.
        That girls play with dolls and scrapbook pictures, and that boys do carpentry if they are not playing with cars, are firmly entrenched attitudes in Norwegian society.
    Usage notes

    Bil commonly refers to a personbil (“passenger car”), but its broader meaning also includes vehicles such as a varebil (“van”) or lastebil (“truck; lorry”). Its scope is therefore wider than that of English car in ordinary usage.

        Swedish

        Swedish Wikipedia has an article on:
        bil
        Wikipedia sv

        Etymology

        From Danish bil.

        Pronunciation

        • IPA(key): /biːl/
        • Audio; “en bil”:(file)
        • Hyphenation: bil
        • Rhymes: -iːl

        Noun

        bil c

        1. a car (automobile)
          köra bil
          drive a car
          åka bil
          ride a car
          köpa bil
          buy a car
          sitta fram / bak i bilen
          sit in the front / back of the car
          Jag tog bilen in till stan och handlade mat
          I took the car into town and picked up groceries [shopped food]
          • 1993, Ronny & Ragge, “Köra fort som fan [Drive fast as hell]”, in Let's Pök! [Let's Bone!]‎:
            Vi ska köra, köra fort som fan. Köra runt med bilen genom hela stan. Vi ska köra, köra fort som fan. Sladda loss och börna genom hela stan ikväll.
            We will [shall] drive, drive fast as hell. Drive around with the car through the whole town. We will drive, drive fast as hell. Drift [skid loose] and burn rubber through the whole town tonight.
        2. a truck (considered a subcategory in Swedish)
          Synonym: lastbil
        3. a van (considered a subcategory in Swedish)
          Synonym: skåpbil

        Usage notes

        A freight truck / lorry is normally qualified as a lastbil, while a pickup truck (pickup) or the like is often simply called a bil ("car") in everyday language (though technically also a lastbil). A freight truck / lorry is the default intuition for lastbil.

        Etymology

        From English beer and German Bier (this deformation was later changed back to the original "r" sound).

        Pronunciation

        • IPA(key): [bil]

        Noun

        bil (genitive bila, plural bils)

        1. bile
        2. (obsolete) beer

        Usage notes

        • (beer): The "l" was later changed to "r" for bir (“beer”).
